findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex, second movement, the paragraph beginning 'The Gospel tells us whose feast it is' (source lines 69-70): 'The Fathers who explained this parable agree that the king is God the Father and that the son is Christ.'
findings.problem: The sentence tells the assembly that the Fathers, as a body, agree on this identification, which is a claim of patristic unanimity. The leaf's evidence does not support that claim, and its own records forbid it. research/scope.md section 1 and the standing limits in research/interpretations.md state that the sweep is bounded and that no reading, author or identification may be called the tradition's or the common view; scope section 4 lists named Matthew commentaries that were never opened, including Origen, Rabanus and the Catena aurea. The expansive study bounds the same point correctly ('These witnesses agree that the king is the Father and the son is Christ', sections/20-the-kings-feast.tex). The homily removes that bound and so asserts a survey that no one performed. The three-document profile forbids inventing unanimity, and the homily-review criteria require precise claims and refuse unsupported attribution.
findings.required_result: Restate the identification so that it covers only witnesses the leaf has checked. Either name Fathers whose loci are in the research records (for example Gregory, Hom. in Evang. 38.3; Jerome, Comm. in Matt. III on 22:2; Hilary, Comm. in Matt. 22.3), or use a plainly bounded phrase such as 'the Fathers we hear from today'. Do not say or imply that all the Fathers, or the tradition, agree. If the repair names a Father the homily does not already cite, add his exact locus to the note's Exact loci and to the References. Then recount the spoken words and update the pace figures in the note and in research/production-review.md.

findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex, first movement, the paragraph beginning 'That is exactly what makes the parable so uncomfortable' (source line 44): 'The word in the Gospel is \emph{neglected}.'
findings.problem: The assembly has just heard the Lectionary's English, which does not use 'neglected' at Mt 22:5. 'Neglected' is the Douay-Rheims word, and it corresponds to Matthew's own Greek and Latin (neglexerunt). Spoken as 'the word in the Gospel', the sentence claims that the Gospel just proclaimed said 'neglected'. A listener who remembers a different word may lose the thread at the point where the homily makes its exegetical turn.
findings.required_result: Attach the word to its source in the speech, for example 'Matthew's word, in the old translation, is neglected', or 'the word Matthew uses means they neglected it'. Do not reproduce the approved Lectionary English.

findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex, fifth movement, the paragraph beginning 'What is that garment?': 'It is not baptism, Augustine says, for the good and the bad alike have been baptized. It is love.'
findings.problem: Augustine's own sentence carries a qualification that the homily drops. At Sermo 90.5 (NPNF Sermon XL) he writes: 'Without Baptism it is true no one attaineth to God; but not every one that hath Baptism attaineth to Him. I cannot therefore understand Baptism ... to be "the wedding garment"'. Without that clause, a Catholic assembly can hear the bare 'It is not baptism' as making baptism unimportant, which is less precise than Augustine is.
findings.required_result: Keep Augustine's qualification in a short spoken clause, for example: 'Not baptism, Augustine says. No one comes to God without it, but the good and the bad alike have been baptized.' Keep the sentence followed, not quoted, as the note says.

findings.location: sections/homily/90-note.tex, 'Relation to the reviewed interpretations', the list of joins that are the homily's own: 'Gregory's \latin{intentus} of the man gone to his farm set beside the Collect's \latin{intentos} on good works (the study's editor's link)'. The same parenthesis appears in research/production-review.md, Derive-homily, as 'the editor's link the study itself names'.
findings.problem: The parenthesis credits the study with more than it says. sections/40-farm-and-merchandise.tex links the Collect's intentos to the attention the invited gave to farm and trade, but it never cites Gregory's 'alius intentus labori terreno' (Hom. in Evang. 38.5). Matching that word to the Collect is the homily's own verbal observation. I checked it, and it is true, but the note's account of where it comes from is inexact.
findings.required_result: Say that the link between the Collect's intentos and the invited's attention to farm and trade is the study's, and that matching it to Gregory's intentus at 38.5 is the homily's own observation of the wording. Make the same correction in the production audit.

summary: Cold review of the homily 'All Things Are Ready' (homily.tex, sections/homily/10-homily.tex and 90-note.tex; packet-sealed hashes confirmed). I read the spoken body through continuously, as a listener would hear it, and then checked it against research/interpretations.md, research/scope.md and the study's 40-farm-and-merchandise and 05-appointed-texts sections. At the tracked loci I checked every quotation and report: the Douay-Rheims verse files for Is 25:6-10, Mt 21:23 and 22:1-14 and Phil 4:10-20; the Clementine at Mt 22:9; NPNF 1/10 Hom. in Matt. 69.1-2; NPNF 1/13 Hom. in Phil. 15; NPNF 1/6 Sermons XL and XLV (Sermo 90.5-6 and 95.7); NPNF 1/8 Enarr. in Ps. 33, sections 13-14; Gregory, Hom. in Evang. 38.3, 5, 6, 9 and 11, in the tracked Latin; and Aquinas, Super Matt. c. 22, on the Venice facsimile, where the sentence stands on p. 281. All quotations are exact, and every locus and section number in the note is correct. Recounted the same way the note counts, the spoken body has 1,452 words, so the stated pace arithmetic holds. The argument is specific to this Sunday and passes the text-substitution test. Its decisive turn comes from Mt 22:5, where the invitation is refused for lawful goods; Philippians 4 and Augustine's 'Clothe others' turn that refusal into a practicable response. The speech observes the Nostra aetate bound, keeps the garment dispute, holds under both forms of the Gospel, and contains no anecdote, clerical identity or composed prayer. One blocking defect remains: the body states that 'the Fathers who explained this parable agree' on an identification, which is a claim of unanimity that the bounded sweep expressly forbids. Limits: no timed or spoken delivery was possible, I made no PDF build or visual check (later stages own those), and I did not compare the Greek or Latin originals of the NPNF English. Verdict: CHANGES_REQUIRED.
